## Abstract

There is societal consensus that cancer clinical trial participation is unjust because some sociodemographic groups have been systematically underrepresented. Despite this, neither a definition nor an ethical explication for the justice norm of equity has been clearly articulated in this setting, leading to confusion over its application and goals. Herein we define equity as acknowledging sociodemographic circumstances and apportioning resource and opportunity allocation to eliminate disparities in outcomes, and we explore the issues and tensions this norm generates through practical examples. We assess how equality-based enrollment structures in clinical cancer research have perpetuated historical disparities and what equity-based alternatives are necessary to achieve representativeness and an expansive conception of participatory justice in clinical cancer research. This framework addresses the breadth from normative to applied by defining the justice norm of equity and translating it into practical strategies for addressing participation disparities in clinical cancer research.

## BACKGROUND AND THEORY

### How Equity and Equality Are Defined in Oncology Research

Equality and equity are overlapping but not synonymous norms of justice. In clinical cancer research, equality, defined as equal opportunity, has been the prevailing standard. Under the auspices of this norm, however, there is ample evidence that patients able to participate in cancer research do not adequately represent those afflicted with cancer, that these differences are largely due to systemic factors and not personal choice, and that there are group-level harms for those less able to participate. This has led to the development of recruitment strategies that promote an outcome-based conception of fairness, colloquially called equity.

Although equality- and equity-based frameworks are oriented in the same direction—toward the ideal of fairness—an equity norm conceives of justice as addressing systemic inequalities and establishing a fairer distribution of resources.1 Equity can be considered value-laden by definition, whereas equality merely references differences between groups.2 For example, older adults do not survive as long after a cancer diagnosis as children. This inequality is not necessarily an inequity because the difference is not generally considered unjust. On a semantic level, the term “health inequity” conveys a lack of fairness rather than a mere lack of sameness. This means that if data suggest that healthcare resource allocation has caused those living farther from hospitals to have decreased healthcare access, leading to shorter survival, this could meet the definition of inequity. In this example, there are differences in both process (access) and outcome (survival) caused by a systemic factor (resource allocation) that could be addressed to improve the process and outcome for those fairing worse. In this case the process and outcome can be labeled inequities both individually and jointly.

A question that is frequently asked as a challenge to equity as a value-laden norm is, to what extent are structural imbalances unfair rather than merely dissimilar? While this is an important question, its framing implies that fair dissimilarity is always the goal, that fair and unfair portions of dissimilarity can be separated, and that the unfair portion can be extirpated. As reviewed below, theory, data, and societal acceptance indicate that unfair structural imbalances exist in clinical oncology research. With this as the basis, and removing the assumptions implied by the question above, we are left with a more practical query: how can fairness be achieved in a system (clinical oncology research) where widespread imbalances are known? The first question reflects the positions of an equality-based research framework, which provides equal opportunity without attending to structural underpinnings, while the second exemplifies an equity-based framework, which accounts for existing variations in patients’ circumstances and seeks fair outcomes.

Another way of conceptualizing equality and equity in the context of clinical cancer research is by analogy. An equality framework would have research institutions allow all potentially eligible patients to participate if they meet the same eligibility criteria and choose to participate, essentially “opening the door” to everyone. In reality, circumstances are such that some individuals may be less likely to participate in clinical trials because they have farther to travel, have less trust in medical research, or are less likely to meet eligibility criteria because of protocol requirements that lack a strict basis in patient safety,3 as elucidated further in subsequent sections, and/or have comorbid conditions related to poor healthcare access.

Each of these barriers to clinical trial participation holds a unique moral weight, and individuals experience their own particular combination of barriers. While the act of “opening the door” signals fairness through equal opportunity, a framework rooted in equity considers systemic social constraints across the patient population. An equity-based framework not only opens the door but also assists patients in reaching and going through it by considering their set of circumstances. In doing so, equity breaks with the process focus of equality, distributing resources differentially in concordance with the unique circumstances of each individual. In other words, equity acknowledges different circumstances and considers proportionate resource and opportunity allocation to eliminate disparities in outcomes.4 For instance, a commitment to equity might be reflected in a hospital’s decision to use a larger portion of its limited resources for participant recruitment to engage with historically underrepresented communities, rebuilding trust and attempting to understand and dissolve the compounding barriers to access experienced by individuals. Practically, equity exists as a tension between process and outcome fairness, straying from process equality (treating all individuals equally with regard to clinical trials access) to the extent that structural unfairness has produced disparities in research participation outcomes. Below, we review the background and implications of disparities in cancer research and identify the normative basis for equity among known theories of justice.

### Participatory Disparities in Clinical Cancer Research

Existing literature identifies differences in clinical cancer research participation across sociodemographic groups that are not justified by established requirements for ethical research conduct.5 Individuals enrolled in oncology clinical trials frequently do not reflect the underlying population diagnosed with a given cancer. Women, historically marginalized racial and ethnic groups, and those from lower socioeconomic strata are often underrepresented because of healthcare access barriers, restrictive clinical trial design and infrastructure, cultural and physical distance between communities and care teams, and bias among clinical investigators.6 There is also understandable patient mistrust of clinical research among historically marginalized populations. This exists in the context of an extensive history of deception, racism, and harm directed toward these groups by the American medical system. Thus, even when offered a clinical trial, some understandably choose not to enroll.7 The goal of oncology clinical research is to eliminate harms related to cancer by identifying life-extending and/or quality-of-life-improving therapies, furthering medicine’s understanding of neoplasia, and offering patients high-quality care.

### Impacts of Inadequate Representation

Inadequate research representation leads to an array of consequences for excluded populations. Although it is debatable whether denial of access to study treatments (and any unproven potential benefits) constitutes harm to the individual, treatments approved based on nongeneralizable populations hold unclear risks and benefits for underrepresented groups.8 Examples of specific harms due to nongeneralizable primary data are reviewed in a later section. Moreover, data absenteeism in correlative research, which identifies promising drug targets and characterizes treatment effects based on patients’ tissue samples, causes future drug development to be biased against sociodemographic groups that cannot participate.9 Even if a particular trial does not provide clinical benefit beyond standard of care, trial care itself is known to be high quality,10 and trial participation offers patients a way to help others.11 Together, these consequences compound existing health disparities, particularly regarding race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status,12 and may propagate lack of trust in research by historically marginalized groups.

Issues of research representation and justice extend across biomedicine. Clinical cancer research epitomizes these broader issues while having idiosyncratic factors, including how germline genetic diversity impacts cancer development, progression, and therapeutic response; how persons with cancer are considered unique by society; and how oncology drug development has distinct regulatory structures. This article attends to both the oncology-specific and disease-agnostic issues of justice in representation.

### Theories of Justice and the Normative Basis for Equity in Clinical Trial Participation

Liberal egalitarianism, capabilities theory, and utilitarianism translate into different approaches for addressing unfairness in the setting of clinical oncology research. In this section, we explicate each of these moral theories and consider the utility of each for promoting justice in oncology clinical trials. Each is relevant for justice in this setting, but there are notable deficiencies when individually applied. A multidimensional moral theory combining procedural- and outcomes-oriented justice may be necessary to address research participation disparities in practice.

Liberal egalitarian theories of justice prominent in modern bioethics consider equal basic liberty and equal opportunity to be central to the idea of fairness.13Liberal egalitarianism, namely the difference principle of Rawlsian justice, permits material inequality as long as fair distribution processes are in place to benefit the least advantaged.14 Through this lens, participatory justice in clinical research suggests that all eligible patients ought to have the opportunity to enroll if they so choose (i.e., justice as fair processes absent outcomes).15 This conception of justice, however, only partially addresses historic and systemic injustices related to research participation in that inequality of opportunity may be necessary for remediation. The difference principle provides guidance for the regulation of social determinants of health, which undergird clinical trial enrollment disparities; however, it falls short of providing the remediation necessary to correct for the historical unfairness of clinical research, the variation of individuals’ experiences prior to their being a participant, or any unfair differences in the outcome of representation. Notably, the difference principle was not intended to offer such directed guidance but rather offer an ideal, theoretical groundwork for ordering a society so that resources are fairly distributed. Rawlsian justice is focused on procedural fairness rather than remediation. Nonetheless, fair opportunity provides a standard against which inequalities of opportunity must be justified if process fairness is considered.

This notion of opportunity is reframed through Nussbaum’s capabilities theory,16 which asserts that individual freedom and dignity stem from having capabilities that allow persons to function both as individuals and within society. Reminiscent of Rawls’s and Daniels’s proceduralism, an opportunity-based capabilities theory applied to oncology clinical research participation asks that individuals have the opportunity to access relevant research studies as a means of achieving normal functioning, or having capabilities met. Nussbaum bridges the liberal egalitarian ideal of equal opportunity to practice by demanding that social arrangements attend to the variability of existence and the need for inequality of opportunity. For example, in oncology clinical trials, Nussbaum’s capabilities theory could potentially require research institutions to provide financial support for travel for patients experiencing geographic barriers to trial participation. In other words, fairness involves ensuring that social arrangements allow all potentially eligible patients to have the opportunity to access clinical trials. Importantly, however, the intention of Nussbaum’s capabilities theory was not to serve as a guide for achieving equity in oncology clinical trials. The subjectivity of capabilities and their valuation, as well as which strategies for participation might be morally permissible (or obligatory) for achieving them, make capabilities theory inadequate as the sole basis for practically addressing unfairness in research participation. Instead, capabilities theory offers a basis for conceptualizing fairness in this setting. In this case, ensuring that individual patient capabilities are met is a prerequisite for fairness.

In contrast to both Rawlsian justice and capabilities theory, utilitarianism frames justice as a common good centered around maximizing utility.17 This perspective challenges clinical research institutions to ensure that research ultimately maximizes benefits for the broader population. Unless they are necessary for maximizing these benefits, however, utilitarianism does not require the dismantling of recurrent systems of oppression that undergird existing clinical trial inequities. Utility-based approaches also allow for vast differences in opportunity, so long as they maximize the broader good. In other words, focusing on maximizing future benefits of research does not necessarily require a restructuring of the clinical research ecosystem through which inadequate representation arose, nor does it require that any semblance of fair opportunity be maintained.

Taken to the extreme, a utilitarian could argue that participation in oncology clinical trials ought to be mandatory for all eligible patients given the potential benefits trials offer for the broader public in terms of safe and efficacious drugs making it to market more rapidly. Given the emphasis placed on respecting individual autonomy in clinical research settings, this argument illustrates one of the downsides of applying utilitarianism here—it allows for individual needs to be disregarded to benefit the greater good.

When applied to the context of oncology clinical research participation, each of these conceptions of justice offers important contributions. Individually, however, they fall short of a singular, clearly defined intervention for improving research representation that considers fairness in both process and outcome while providing practical means for attainment. In this context, we advocate for a multidimensional approach to justice in oncology clinical trials through the lens of equity. This approach considers justice to be an amalgam of both fair processes (meaning fairness in all elements of trial recruitment) and fair outcomes (meaning the actual participation rates). Equity in this context begins with the ideal of process fairness and strays from it exactly to the extent that systemic injustices have produced disparities in research participation outcomes. It exists in and as the tension between process fairness and outcome fairness, accepting process inequality insofar as it corrects for structural injustice and to the degree that it realizes outcome fairness.

Armed with this multidimensional approach, the next steps are to further delineate the concept of equity and how it relates to the established equality norm, elucidate how procedural fairness and outcome-based fairness can conflict, and show how equality-based enrollment practices have perpetuated disparities. These lead to a natural exploration of the ethical and practical ramifications of interventions to enhance research equity, including the distribution of trials, the use of enrollment quotas, and the use of participant payments.

### Current Applications of Equity and Equality in Oncology Clinical Trials

Many solutions proposed to address research participation disparities have been based on an equality norm. In oncology, this yielded processes such as eliminating arbitrary eligibility criteria and uniform remuneration for the burdens and risk of participation. From the 1990s through the early 2010s, enaction and revision of laws and statutes, including 21 C.F.R. 56,18 codified that all participants were to be “selected equitably,” with identification of and protections for specific vulnerable populations. While properly intentioned, equitable selection led to legal and ethical concerns that justice as equal opportunity would be violated by providing patients with contextually appropriate support to avail themselves of research opportunities.

Relatedly, others have argued that the labeling of and protections for “vulnerable populations” have substantially impaired health for these persons because of the logistics required to include them in research,19 an unintended and ironic violation of process equality. An example of this is the routine exclusion of pregnant persons from clinical research despite substantial evidence of predicted risks for this group. Such exclusion ultimately results in knowledge gaps that inhibit the medical community from caring for pregnant persons optimally. Inclusion of these groups necessitates a shift from labeling them as a vulnerable population requiring protection to autonomous human beings with a distinct set of needs.20

The equality norm has also reinforced the notion that if each organization involved in research (e.g., an institution such as a pharmaceutical company) individually provides equal opportunity, the system of research is emergently equal. This notion aligns well with the distributed nature of clinical research, where there are many organizations involved with distinct responsibilities and goals. This is disruptively atomistic: it requires organizations to only consider opportunity fairness as it applies to their own involvement rather than from the perspective of the participant and in relation to other participating organizations, the history of related research, and society.

For instance, in keeping with the norm of equality, a hospital could implement an internal process for identifying all potentially eligible participants for a trial by reviewing medical records of existing patients and mandate that treating physicians inform all potentially eligible participants about the availability of the trial. However, this strategy fails to consider that potentially eligible participants may not have been able to access the hospital owing to inadequate means of transportation, absence of health insurance, or lack of trust in the institution or in related research. Moreover, the commitment to equality does not challenge the hospital to consider how all participating sites could, both separately and jointly, engage with historically underrepresented communities.

In contrast, an equity norm attempts to account for historical and social structures through which individuals enter the realm of clinical research. It works toward the remediation of outcome differences between groups and communities considered to be unfair. For example, through an equity norm, clinical trial eligibility criteria would be examined for their process fairness and their impact on enrollment opportunities across groups, and an equity norm would assess whether differences in impact are justifiable. An argument against this conception of equity is that it requires subjective valuations of what is contextually appropriate and how resources are distributed. The question of who ought to be making such subjective valuations also remains. A rebuttal is that equity-based research interventions are morally obligatory attempts to combat underlying systems of oppression that have created disparities in healthcare and health outcomes, and that subjective valuations of resource distribution occur ubiquitously in the real world but do not often address ongoing systemic barriers to care and trial participation. To address the question of who ought to make such subjective valuations, continuous engagement with underrepresented communities is a critical component of equity-based research interventions.

Through its basis in history, society, and culture, equity-based research interventions are built as multidimensional, coordinated approaches that respond to the multitude of factors contributing to participatory disparities. Despite these differences, equity and equality are distinct but not mutually exclusive concepts. Their overlap can be easily seen when assessing the major factors contributing to participatory disparities.

### Factors Contributing to Participatory Disparities and How They Relate to Fairness

Structural and clinical factors constitute some of the main contributors to disparities in research participation, as shown in table 1. Structural factors span structures across society (e.g., variable health insurance) and within the clinical research enterprise (e.g., clinical trial site locations). Although there has been some “decentralization” of research in recent years,21 meaning that patients can have some of their participation occur virtually or at a local hospital, clinical trials are most frequently conducted at large institutions where infrastructure has been built to handle the burdens of research administration and regulatory oversight. Many of the enrollment barriers are extensions of larger social issues, such as general impediments in access to healthcare, as well as structural racism, genderism and sexism, classism, and many isms beyond.

In contrast, clinical factors include trial design and attitudinal issues. The latter can affect both clinical trialists and potential enrollees, but the actual impact is unclear. One of the most commonly cited examples is underrepresented patient groups’ lack of trust in clinical cancer research and their corresponding unwillingness to participate; however, studies have demonstrated that this may account for only a small proportion of disparate enrollment compared to structural factors or researchers’ implicit bias (i.e., their perception that a variety of historically marginalized groups are less ideal candidates for research participation).22 Participant compliance is critical for ensuring robust data collection and to promote participant safety. As such, researchers may hold implicit bias toward participants they assume might demonstrate noncompliance. Indeed, some clinical researchers can hold incorrect beliefs that racial and ethnic minorities are potentially noncompliant and thus less ideal trial participants.23

Prior literature on clinical cancer research disparities has focused on siloed implementation of equality-based solutions by outlining strategies researchers can utilize within the confines of a particular study.24 In contrast, more recent equity-based approaches consider participatory fairness across the population burdened by the cancer and within which trials exist.25 This can include accountability measures to ensure that sites and sponsors are meeting goals of representation for individual trials and across their portfolios. Another example of a multilevel strategy is the use of community engagement to discuss individual trial design, implementation, and findings while also fostering a sense of trust between the clinical research site and the surrounding community.26 Such approaches seek to account for the variability of patients’ circumstances, attempting to achieve both fair processes and fair outcomes. They target structural and clinical barriers through a reorganization of the clinical research infrastructure to meet the needs of all members of the target disease population.27

## ETHICAL AND PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS OF AN EQUITY-BASED NORM

Numerous strategies for reducing participatory disparities exist, from patient education to navigation to outreach.28 In this section we consider issues related to the equity norm for selected strategies. Strategies were chosen as exemplars of a particular ethical issue and to span all levels of influence identified in the National Institute for Minority Health and Health Disparities’ Research Framework.29 These strategies and levels of influence are shown in figure 1. We also consider who bears responsibility for equity in clinical cancer research and what steps are being taken in that regard. Though we consider this span of issues to reflect how equity interventions address unfairness in a holistic sense, we recognize that health equity cannot be achieved by merely following strategies aimed at mitigating cancer research participation disparities but health equity demands broader structural and societal reform that extends beyond the scope of this article.

### Rigorous Enrollment and Representative Enrollment

A useful way of conceptualizing equality and equity in the context of cancer research participation is to view equality as a commitment to a so-called “rigorous enrollment” strategy and equity as a commitment to a “representative enrollment” strategy. Some have argued that enrollment in clinical trials should be guided entirely by biology and pharmacology, meaning that exclusion criteria should be solely based on known or suspected safety signals and preclinical and clinical data showing that the malignancy or the trial drug acts differently across different groups.30 For instance, one might want to exclude patients with particular genetic ancestries in a dose-finding study because the class of drug is known to be processed differently by a large proportion of that group, and their inclusion would lead to inaccurate dosing because the target population is largely of a different ancestry. This approach also implies that trials should continue to operate at high-enrolling centers that can quickly and rigorously screen and enroll patients. We refer to this strategy as “rigorous enrollment.”

This equality-based process is largely practiced now. It implies that fairness in oncology clinical trials means equal opportunity by preventing the arbitrary exclusion of patients and that the practical challenges of enrollment—where less than 5 percent of eligible patients are enrolled31—can be overcome by dedicating resources to optimizing infrastructure at key sites. Such measures include increased administrative support and process improvements (e.g., systemic patient review to identify and screen eligible patients). These efforts are aimed at improving enrollment rates overall, rather than focusing particularly on historically underrepresented populations. The fairness argument for this strategy is that it allows for fast and successful enrollment, completion of testing, and quicker attainment of regulatory approval, making commercial drugs available for the entire population sooner. Advocates for this strategy argue that data on unenrolled groups can be obtained through retrospective investigations of real-world data after approval.

The differential access to medicine within the U.S. healthcare system and its history of structural racism suggest that trial enrollment processes driven by biology and pharmacology alone do not reflect fairness.32 Those supporting this position argue that researchers and policymakers must acknowledge existing inequities within the clinical research infrastructure and craft solutions that address the multitude of factors leading to participatory disparities. In an effort to reckon with the reality of such disparities, some argue that “good science does not mean divorcing experience from research,”33 implying that fair research conduct involves a conscious redesign of research infrastructure so that it does not exclude historically marginalized groups.

Within this framework, there is clear tension between enrolling patients as quickly as possible regardless of their demographic profile, under the presumption that it quickens accrual and saves more lives, and enrolling patients equitably under the presumption that benefits of future developments would be more fairly distributed. We term the latter strategy the “representative enrollment” approach. In an effort to promote representative enrollment, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Food and Drug Amendments of 2022 requiring sponsors seeking U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to provide the FDA with diversity plans for achieving representative participation.34 Although this policy lacks details on how adequate representation will be defined and to what degree it will be enforced, it serves as a useful starting point for conceptualizing equity in the context of cancer clinical trials.35

Two arguments supporting “representative enrollment” are as follows: (1) rigorous enrollment may lead to approvals that are less safe or effective for underenrolled groups,36 and (2) post-approval studies may only show these differences after medically underserved groups are already harmed. One example of this is a commonly used breast cancer recurrence risk score (Oncotype DX) used to decide whether chemotherapy is needed after surgery. The pivotal clinical trial for this test underenrolled Black women, and a decade later studies found that there was increased relapse and decreased overall survival for Black women when they had the same score as non-Hispanic White women. It is difficult not to conclude that if Black women had been representatively enrolled, their scores would have been more accurate for them, potentially directing more of them to receive chemotherapy and reducing relapse.37

Proponents of representative enrollment also note that promoting representativeness does not inherently slow trial accrual or scientific advancement and that arguments presuming this inherently deprioritize the health of already-marginalized communities.38 Moreover, if previously unsupported groups are supported in their ability to enroll, the number of potential participants grows, and representative enrollment may actually become faster than rigorous enrollment. An additional argument stems from the inequitable diffusion of innovation that has occurred when trials are conducted away from centers that treat marginalized groups.39 This leads to clinicians who take longer to incorporate novel therapies into their practice and are less familiar with their delivery and toxicity when they do, further diminishing post-approval safety and efficacy. Given that an equity-based framework has been absent from the cancer research infrastructure until recently,40 the assertion that representative enrollment would lack speed or rigor is speculative.

### Clinical Trial Distribution

Current regulations in the United States do not require aligning the distribution of oncology trials with the cancer burden of the population: the type, number, and goals of trials are not planned or distributed to match the disease spectrum from prevention to detection, treatment, palliation, and survivorship. In addition, there are few geographic, sociodemographic, or other dimensions of trial regulation aligning disease with patient. This leads to multiple trials recruiting the same subset of patients from the same areas and with the same cancer state and few or no trials in other subsets. Current mechanisms to align trial distribution with burden are indirect through federal funding and do not impact trials sponsored by private entities.

Despite a limited societal approach, some community and organizational trial interventions are being tested and/or implemented to varying degrees. These include decentralizing portions of or whole trials such that patients can access research where they are or at a local facility,41 identifying barriers in access and enrollment to high-enrolling centers such that “rational site development” can identify how to open a nationally representative trial ahead of time based on past site accrual, and understanding how patients flow from community centers to academic centers at later stages of their disease.

In many instances trial distribution reflects the power imbalance of clinical research in that efforts to align trials with disease burden are resource intensive and/or seek to disrupt the current structure of clinical cancer research at the expense of sponsors and traditional research institutions. While not a direct regulatory approach, indirect ways of supporting these efforts are to increase and include governmental and philanthropic funding directed toward trial decentralization and previously underfunded cancers and disease states with large, documented disparities, as well as nonbinding FDA guidance to demographically match trials with disease burden. Strategies include enrollment quotas, participant payments, and focusing on relative expenditures.

### Enrollment Quotas

Enrollment quotas are predefined accrual targets based on some dimension of representation for previously underenrolled groups, such as reserving 20 percent of enrollment slots for persons who identify as Hispanic. A normative concern for quotas is that they are exclusions unsupported by participant safety (and/or biology) and therefore represent an unjustified reason to stop an otherwise-eligible patient from enrolling. A counterargument is that this may be balanced by the additional safety information obtained by purposefully enrolling previously underrepresented populations.

A more tenable approach to the quota may be the “extension arm” approach—that is, opening additional slots structured to preferentially assess a disease state or therapeutic approach more likely to enroll previously underenrolled groups without specific restrictions based on demographics. This approach obviates concerns over subjects being barred from participation due to social constructs such as race. Instead, it investigates a question of scientific value for historically marginalized groups. An example of this is a bone marrow transplant trial with a specific extension arm for haplo-identical donor transplantation, meaning a donor who is immunologically half-matched to the patient (typically a first-degree relative). This type of transplantation is more commonly used for persons with African or multi-continental ancestry where other donor types are limited, but its use has only recently increased owing to improvements in toxicity and supportive care. Further discussion is warranted around the logistical and ethical considerations of utilizing enrollment quotas in both implementation and regulation.

### Participant Payments

Participant payments shift financial burdens from patients to sponsoring pharmaceutical companies and participating hospitals. Payments can remunerate for direct or indirect costs or for the risks associated with participation; controversially, payments can also incentivize participation and may even be seen as coercive if they ameliorate material hardship often seen in marginalized groups. Payments may reflect participatory equity if they allow those who would not otherwise be able to participate to do so. Opponents of such strategies argue that payments run the risk of backfiring, increasing concerns over furthering mistrust between traditionally underrepresented populations and research institutions.42

Reimbursement of direct costs may include monetary expenses incurred related to participation, such as travel expenses for trial-related clinic appointments and hospitalizations. Reimbursement of indirect costs may include recompense for lost wages from work, caregiver time and lost wages, and increased childcare costs. Reimbursement for the risk associated with participation can pay for either assumed risk or direct injury, though the latter is uncommon. Risk reimbursement is also practically difficult to disentangle from the final form of payment, incentivizing payments, which controversially offer compensation for those willing to participate.

Reimbursement for direct costs is the least contentious in that it is fiscally neutral and thus not considered incentivizing. Direct cost reimbursement reflects the norm of equity, as the amount of reimbursement varies with an individual’s cost of participation. In practice, however, challenges remain in identifying an individual’s cost of participation given each person’s unique set of circumstances. Reimbursements for indirect costs and research-related risk are more controversial in that there is no clear scope for indirect costs. Moreover, there is little guidance on what degree of reimbursement is acceptable, whether all participants should receive payment, and whether payment is need independent (i.e., equal) or need based (i.e., equitable).

Additional issues arise when a trial is financially constrained from being able to completely reimburse individuals for any payment type. The issues surrounding payment should be considered at the trial budgeting stage such that participants are informed regarding payments at the time of consent. Potential options include remuneration restrictions (e.g., only reimbursing for certain direct costs), caps, and need-based distribution.

Generally, an enrollment approach that meets the procedural norm of equity would offer direct, indirect, and risk-associated cost reimbursement for all participants with limits to guard against perversion of such payments that would not allow the outcome norm of equity to be fulfilled. Any practical reimbursement scheme would need to have caps, especially for indirect and risk-associated payments. Such caps would guard against concerns over coercion, the perversion of indirect payments for affluent individuals, unduly burdening the sponsor, and avoiding payment levels that would disqualify disadvantaged individuals from other need-based support. One such scheme could include prespecified direct cost reimbursement for travel, childcare, lodging (if needed), meals, and parking; indirect cost reimbursement as a set amount of payment for work hours lost, if not already compensated by their workplace; and a set payment for research-associated risk that all parties incur.

Need-based distribution of payment for indirect cost is increasingly being considered as the payment-associated mechanism to overcome socioeconomic disparities in research participation.43 Such compensation arguably fits both the process and outcome ends of the equity norm, as it overcomes the difficulties in participation faced by those with less means with the intention of ensuring that trial results are generalizable to people similar to them. At face value, providing varying amounts of compensation to participants violates the equality norm, but such unequal payments are arguably permissible in certain circumstances. Neglecting to provide participant payment for indirect costs creates an additional barrier to enrollment for patients of lower socioeconomic strata. In this context, such a barrier to entry can be considered a form of discrimination based on socioeconomic status. Especially when distributing limited reimbursement funds to promote enrollment of a generalizable population, need-based distribution of payments for indirect costs may be morally permissible—and perhaps even morally obligatory—if equity is the norm to be upheld. It is worth reiterating that indirect cost payments are reimbursement and not purely for the purposes of incentivizing. While this notion might invoke concerns over unfairness since, in an ideal setting, anyone who participates should receive equal financial support, trial budgets are such that this is often impossible.

Another tier of payment involves outright provision of funds beyond the direct and indirect expenses incurred while enrolled in the study. This type of payment is more common for phase 1 clinical trials with healthy volunteers outside of oncology, but it has been considered less ethically acceptable in cancer research because of the cost of cancer care and because marginalized populations are more likely to be financially vulnerable.44 Even with healthy volunteers, participant payments present potential concerns of individual and undue inducement, participant exploitation, and data validity.45 However, given that participating in clinical cancer research presents added risk to the participant for the ultimate benefit of a future public if a drug is approved, an argument can be made that participant payments are fair because they acknowledge the risk participants are taking and their contribution to society. Moreover, the specter of “ethical concerns” over coercion allows sponsors and research sites to sidestep participant payments altogether without careful deliberation as to whether payments are truly ethically obligatory, optional, or prohibited. When institutional review boards approve of a trial, they are acknowledging that trial to be socially valuable and safe for participants. Thus, payments for incentivization may be justified to promote its success.46

Finally, even if the intention of participant payment is to provide reimbursement rather than incentivization, researchers and sponsors should recognize that the distinction might not always be obvious to participants. Some scholars note that payments present a slippery slope toward exploitation and undue inducement, thus failing to acknowledge the cautionary lessons learned from the Tuskegee syphilis study;47 however, others are more concerned with underpaying participants, insisting that failure to pay fairly runs the risk of hindering trial recruitment, creating further financial barriers to enrollment, and failing to acknowledge the contributions of each participant.48 Given the complexities surrounding fairness, it is critical that payment decisions only be made after careful deliberation with patients and historically marginalized groups, avoiding paternalistic judgments of what might serve their best interests. Further empirical research is warranted to assess how different forms of payment or reimbursement might affect decision-making.

### Healthcare Expenditure

Another financial concern related to participatory equity in clinical cancer research is overall expenditure. While relative economic loss or gain may not appear prima facie relevant, clinical trials are not an abundantly available resource. In this way the novel therapies they provide constitute a limited and heterogeneously distributed resource, making relative expenditures worth considering insofar as they impact availability and distribution. Data from the National Academies of Medicine argue that failing to maintain population representativeness in oncology clinical trials will ultimately increase healthcare expenditure.49 Their models predict that population health disparities due to enrollment inequity will be more expensive than upfront financial costs of equitable enrollment. Moreover, some research suggests that incentive payments can boost accrual to clinical trials without violating principles of voluntary informed consent,50 and that modifying infrastructure to promote representative participation is fiscally untenable, though who pays remains an ongoing debate.

Overall expenditure arguments attend to the consequentialist basis of equity, as promoting representative enrollment appears cost-effective and has the potential to improve overall health outcomes. At the same time, the upfront cost of representative enrollment places value on expanding the opportunity structures through which patients access clinical research. This attention to the circumstances of patients simultaneously reflects a deontological appreciation for patients as ends in and of themselves, underscoring the multidimensional approach of equity as fair process and outcomes. It also speaks to the broader notion of equity that demands that clinical research do more than merely “open the door” to potential enrollees.

### Who Bears Responsibility?

While existing strategies largely focus on actions that can be taken by an institution or within a trial, such as patient education, increased screening, and patient navigation,51 the moral obligation of pharmaceutical sponsors and policymakers to uphold an equity norm should necessarily be at least as large in scope as the research they conduct or regulate. Given the evidence that disparities in clinical cancer research participation arise from a multitude of factors,52 it is critical that frameworks for addressing participation disparities use multilevel approaches and engage relevant stakeholders, including patients, study teams, sponsors, and regulators.53

As an example, the FDA and research partners have begun promoting the norm of equity throughout the drug development process.54 Initially developed as proposed guidance, the new Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022 now mandates diversity plans for oncology clinical trials and targets for representation.55 Pre-FDA approval examples include eliminating eligibility criteria that are not based on drug safety, outlining site- and study-specific enrollment diversity plans, and/or utilizing diversity officers to monitor for disparities and correct for them in real time. Post-approval, the FDA recommends complementary rather than supplementary real-world data analyses to ensure safety and efficacy across groups.56 For example, one of the primary objectives of a post-approval therapeutic trial for multiple myeloma, which disproportionately affects African American men, could be to utilize real-world data to fill in gaps of underrepresentation in preapproval clinical trials. The real-world data in this example are complementary in that they are an integral component of the post-approval trial, rather than being merely an extra or exploratory objective. While there is increasing agreement with such strategies, debate remains around how to enforce such recommendations and what are acceptable endpoints for representation, which is multidimensional and intersectional. These steps, while significant in shifting oncology research norms from equality to equity, continue to consider equipoise in terms of individual trials, leaving a gap in FDA oversight with respect to fairness across the population.

## LIMITATIONS

It is critical to note that the equity-based solutions discussed herein are merely starting points for the work of justice in clinical cancer research. Further discussion will necessitate incorporating the perspectives of relevant stakeholders, including traditionally underrepresented voices such as those from historically marginalized communities. In anticipation of potential criticism, it is worth reemphasizing that the implementation of an equity-based framework requires continued attention to the individual circumstances surrounding patients without tokenization. It is critical that historically marginalized voices are incorporated into conversations around fair representation in oncology clinical trials. Additionally, even if purely equity-based norms were to be utilized, they would not absolve the need for broader equity-based healthcare reform beyond the clinical oncology research setting. Ongoing research and community engagement are needed to inform clinical researchers and policymakers of how patients make sense of their cancer diagnosis, how patients perceive clinical research institutions, and how research institutions can meet all of their patients’ needs more effectively. Moreover, social, economic, and political factors underlie lack of access to trials, and accordingly each of these sectors requires attention. Another anticipated criticism exists around the choice to embrace multidimensionality in defining justice rather than tethering it to a single moral theory or principle. While multidimensionality can yield incompatibility, our aim is to begin addressing an existing gap in the literature by translating moral theory and ethical norms into the ongoing practice and policy changes being adopted in oncology clinical trials. Rather than generating a formulaic framework with absolute coherence, we intend to initiate a nuanced discussion around the ethical and practical implications of various strategies that have been and are being implemented to remediate participatory inequities in clinical cancer research.

## CONCLUSION

Through a multidimensional lens of justice as both fair process and fair outcomes, improving clinical cancer research representation is a moral imperative. In order to actualize ideal commitments to justice, such as those brought forth by liberal egalitarianism and utilitarianism, an equity-based norm appreciates the necessary interplay between process and outcomes. As process fairness and outcome fairness differ, the equity norm of justice can exist as conflict between the two. Equity necessitates straying from process equality to the extent that systemic injustices have produced disparities in participation outcomes. In other words, a commitment to equity involves an adherence to procedural fairness unless and until it detracts from outcome fairness. This tension reflects fairness in the real world and subverts the deficiencies of individual moral theories focused on process or outcome alone. Participation equity in cancer research would allow for access to novel therapies and ensure that their development would benefit the broader population, especially those who have been historically marginalized. Grounding representative participation in the norm of equity as opposed to equality demands that the field of oncology clinical research move beyond siloed attempts to remediate single trials or institutions. Instead, equity challenges oncology clinical research to restructure itself in a way that attends to the needs and circumstances of individual patients, with special consideration given to those who have been historically marginalized. Further deliberation, in conversation with social science research and incorporating the perspectives of relevant stakeholders, including traditionally underrepresented voices, is warranted. Such efforts will bridge the gap from the circumstances, experiences, and perspectives of oncology patients to the policy, practices, and infrastructure of clinical research in order to address the unfairness of participatory inequities in oncology clinical research.

## Abstract

What are oncologists’ views on ethical issues associated with the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in cancer care?

In this cross-sectional survey study, 84.8% of US oncologists reported that AI needs to be explainable by oncologists but not necessarily patients, and 81.4% agreed that patients should consent to AI use for cancer treatment decisions. Less than half (47.1%) of oncologists viewed medico-legal problems from AI use as physicians’ responsibility, and although most (76.5%) reported feeling responsible for protecting patients from biased AI, few (27.9%) reported feeling confident in their ability to do so.

This study suggests that concerns about ethical issues, including explainability, patient consent, and responsibility, may impede optimal adoption of AI into cancer care.

## Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly integrating into cancer care. Understanding stakeholder views on ethical issues associated with the implementation of AI in oncology is critical to optimal deployment.

To evaluate oncologists’ views on the ethical domains of the use of AI in clinical care, including familiarity, predictions, explainability (the ability to explain how a result was determined), bias, deference, and responsibilities.

This cross-sectional, population-based survey study was conducted from November 15, 2022, to July 31, 2023, among 204 US-based oncologists identified using the National Plan & Provider Enumeration System.

The primary outcome was response to a question asking whether participants agreed or disagreed that patients need to provide informed consent for AI model use during cancer treatment decisions.

Of 387 surveys, 204 were completed (response rate, 52.7%). Participants represented 37 states, 120 (63.7%) identified as male, 128 (62.7%) as non-Hispanic White, and 60 (29.4%) were from academic practices; 95 (46.6%) had received some education on AI use in health care, and 45.3% (92 of 203) reported familiarity with clinical decision models. Most participants (84.8% [173 of 204]) reported that AI-based clinical decision models needed to be explainable by oncologists to be used in the clinic; 23.0% (47 of 204) stated they also needed to be explainable by patients. Patient consent for AI model use during treatment decisions was supported by 81.4% of participants (166 of 204). When presented with a scenario in which an AI decision model selected a different treatment regimen than the oncologist planned to recommend, the most common response was to present both options and let the patient decide (36.8% [75 of 204]); respondents from academic settings were more likely than those from other settings to let the patient decide (OR, 2.56; 95% CI, 1.19-5.51). Most respondents (90.7% [185 of 204]) reported that AI developers were responsible for the medico-legal problems associated with AI use. Some agreed that this responsibility was shared by physicians (47.1% [96 of 204]) or hospitals (43.1% [88 of 204]). Finally, most respondents (76.5% [156 of 204]) agreed that oncologists should protect patients from biased AI tools, but only 27.9% (57 of 204) were confident in their ability to identify poorly representative AI models.

In this cross-sectional survey study, few oncologists reported that patients needed to understand AI models, but most agreed that patients should consent to their use, and many tasked patients with choosing between physician- and AI-recommended treatment regimens. These findings suggest that the implementation of AI in oncology must include rigorous assessments of its effect on care decisions as well as decisional responsibility when problems related to AI use arise.

## Abstract

This cross-sectional survey study evaluates oncologists’ views on the ethical domains of the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical care, including familiarity, predictions, explainability, bias, deference, and responsibilities.

## Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is an emerging set of technologies with the potential to advance cancer discovery and care delivery.1 Artificial intelligence models with applications for oncology have recently been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA),2 and the increasing complexity of personalized cancer care makes the field of oncology poised for an AI revolution. Concerns have been raised over AI bias, explainability (ie, the ability of an AI model to explain how it reached a result), responsibility for error or misuse, and humans’ deference to its results.3,4,5 As the ethical deployment of AI in cancer care requires solutions that meet the needs of stakeholders, this study sought to examine oncologists’ familiarity with AI and perspectives on these issues. As familiarity with a technology changes stakeholder perceptions of it,6 and because academic research in AI is burgeoning, we hypothesized that responses would vary for oncologists practicing in academic settings compared with those in other practice settings.

## Methods

From November 15, 2022, to July 31, 2023, we performed a cross-sectional survey study of oncologists practicing in the US. A draft instrument based on published ethical frameworks4,5 was developed by a team of oncologists, survey methodologists, bioethicists, and AI researchers (A.H., T.P.W., J.M.M., K.L.K., R.S., E.V.A., and G.A.A.). The instrument was iteratively refined through cognitive testing with 5 practicing oncologists until meaning saturation was achieved. The final instrument (eMethods in Supplement 1) contained 24 questions including demographics and the following domains: AI familiarity, predictions, explainability, bias, deference, and responsibilities. A random sample of oncologists was identified using the National Plan & Provider Enumeration System (eMethods in Supplement 1).7 Recruitment methods followed best practices,8 using mailed paper surveys with gift cards ($25), after which reminder letters with an electronic survey option and telephone calls were used for nonresponders. The study was approved by the Dana-Farber Office for Human Research Studies. We received a waiver of written documentation of consent from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute institutional review board. The survey instrument was introduced with a clear consent statement (a full page on paper and a full screen in the electronic version) describing the study, its voluntary nature, the participant’s rights, and what participation entailed. Completing the survey constituted consent to participate in the study. This study followed the CROSS guidelines9 (eMethods in Supplement 1).

Responses were grouped for analysis as shown in the eMethods in Supplement 1. The χ2 test or the Fisher exact test assessed bivariate associations between responses and primary practice (academic hospital or clinic [“academic”] vs other), with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs reported. The primary outcome was respondent views on the need for patients to provide informed consent for the use of an AI model during treatment decision-making. A multivariable logistic regression model assessed associations between respondent characteristics with the primary outcome; covariates with P ≤ .05 in bivariate testing were included. These covariates included sociodemographic characteristics (including self-reported race and ethnicity [racial and ethnic group categories were aligned with National Institutes of Health reporting guidelines under NOT-OD-15-089; race and ethnicity were assessed because a number of AI tools have been shown to perpetuate bias and racism that inordinately affects minoritized racial and ethnic groups]), practice setting, and prior training, defined as previous AI-specific education (eg, courses and lectures). Imputation was planned if question missingness was more than 5%. All P values were 2-sided; the significance level was P < .05 unless otherwise specified. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata, version 16 (StataCorp LLC).

## Results

Of 399 mailed surveys, 12 were undeliverable, and 204 were completed (response rate, 52.7%); question missingness was less than 1%. Participants represented 37 states, 120 (63.7%) identified as male, 128 (62.7%) identified as non-Hispanic White, and 60 (29.4%) were from academic practices; 109 (53.4%) had no prior AI training, and 45.3% (92 of 203) reported familiarity with clinical decision models (Table 1). Although 93.1% (189 of 203) reported that they would benefit from dedicated training, 75.0% (153 of 204) did not know of appropriate resources. eTables 1 to 4 in Supplement 1 show familiarity, predictions, and acceptability of AI models. Those in academic practices were more likely than those in other settings to report they could explain AI pathology models (OR, 2.08; 95% CI, 1.06-4.12). They were also more likely to predict that AI would improve adverse effect management (OR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.01-3.73) and end-of-life decision-making (OR, 2.06; 95% CI, 1.11-3.84).

## Discussion

In this nationally representative, cross-sectional survey study assessing oncologists’ views on ethical issues associated with AI in cancer care, we found associations between practice setting and AI-related predictions, deference, and explainability. Most participants reported that patients should consent to the use of AI during treatment decision-making, and those without prior training were more likely to view consent as necessary. Responses about decision-making were sometimes paradoxical; patients were not expected to understand AI tools but were expected make decisions related to recommendations generated by AI. A gap was also seen between oncologist responsibilities and preparedness to combat AI-related bias. Together, these data characterize barriers that may impede the ethical adoption of AI into cancer care.

There is relatively little known about AI’s clinical implementation issues as they relate to clinical stakeholders.10 Our findings begin to bridge AI development with the expectations of end users so that tools can be appropriately applied. For example, oncologists’ knowledge and training were relatively uncommon compared with self-reported obligations to patients and deference to AI. This finding complements normative discussions about the erosion of human responsibilities through AI overreliance11 and brings up the question about whether such responsibilities will always be necessary. This aligns with our finding that few respondents assumed responsibility for the medico-legal problems stemming from AI recommendations.

### Limitations

This study has some limitations, including the moderate sample size and response rate, although cohort demographics appear to be nationally representative.12,13 In addition, responses to specific use cases and thresholds for using AI may differ from the general perceptions identified. Psychometrically validated AI-focused survey instruments were not available, but pretesting was used to enhance face and content validity. Finally, the cross-sectional nature of these data limits generalizability over time as AI is integrated into cancer care.

## Conclusions

Ethical AI in cancer care requires accounting for stakeholder positions. This cross-sectional survey study highlights potential issues related to accountability and deference to AI as well as associations with practice setting. Our findings suggest that the implementation of AI in the field of oncology must include rigorous assessments of its effect on care decisions and decisional responsibility when problems related to AI use arise.
