# Establishing and Defining an Approach to Climate Conscious Clinical Medical Ethics

**Authors:** Andrew Hantel; Jonathan M. Marron; Gregory A. Abel

**Affiliations:** aDana-Farber Cancer Institute; | bHarvard Medical School

## Abstract

An anthropocentric scope for clinical medical ethics (CME) has largely separated this area of bioethics from environmental concerns. In this article, we first identify and reconcile the ethical issues imposed on CME by climate change including the dispersion of related causes and effects, the transdisciplinary and transhuman nature of climate change, and the historic divorce of CME from the environment. We then establish how several moral theories undergirding modern CME, such as virtue ethics, feminist ethics, and several theories of justice, promote both a flourishing of human medical practice and the environment. We conclude by defining an expanded the scope of CME as inclusive of not only patients, families, physicians, and other health professionals but other humans, non-humans, and their shared environment. We then apply this scope and theory to a widely used framework for applying CME, the Four Topics model, to construct a climate conscious approach to CME.

## Background

If greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions continue at present rates, global warming will increase >4°C by 2100.1 Emissions propagate ecologic disaster through sea-level rise, pollution, and drought. Experts anticipate that human health will suffer greatly, with those from low- and middle-income countries and marginalized groups most affected.2,3 Human beings have also triggered a mass extinction of flora and fauna through an extractive relationship with the Earth.4 The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) found that obviating the worst impacts of climate change requires limiting warming to <1.5°C. Indeed, the human mortality cost associated with the difference between 1.5 and 2°C warming is staggering: an estimated additional 300 million deaths by 2100 in the best-case scenario and 3 billion in the worst-case.5 Even the best case represents more deaths than those from all wars in the 20th century.6 This estimate also does not encompass the biotic and planetary costs, which are even more astonishing in scope. As the IPPC states, “rapid, far-reaching and unprecedented changes [are needed] in all aspects of society” to address this crisis and preserve our world.1

Clinical medical ethics (CME) is the prototypically anthropocentric branch of bioethics. Its focus has been human medical practice, with a goal of “[helping] patients, families, physicians, and other health professionals reach good clinical decisions by taking into account both the specific clinical situation and the patient’s values and preferences.”7 To date, CME has largely separated human health from environmental concerns. This dualism raises two central questions that we seek to address. Are these global, diffusely biotic, and intergenerational problems of climate change reconcilable with an ethic guiding human medical practice? If so, from which moral grounding can a climate conscious CME promote both a flourishing of human health and the environment?

In this paper, we outline how climate change is a problem applicable to CME, and we argue that CME has largely failed to address this existential threat. We then characterize how some of the same moral theories upon which CME is based address this threat, exposing the artificial gap between theory and practice. With this gap as our basis, we establish a revised scope for CME, and we formulate a practical approach to this revised scope based on Jonsen and Siegler’s popular Four Topics model.7

## The Ethical and Clinical Medical Problems of Climate Change

Anthropogenic climate change is a transdisciplinary problem involving the physical and life sciences, economics, and international relations, among others. Climate change is also an intrinsically ethical issue as decisions and actions can mitigate or propagate climate-related harms. There are human and non-human interests, potential virtues and responsibilities, and related choices. The environment is intimately connected to clinical medicine. Human disease risk, acquisition, progression, and management are modulated by interactions with non-human biota and our shared ecosystem.8 If there are both ethical and clinical medical relationships to the environment and human health, might clinical medical ethics also relate to the environment?

In this section, we establish the relationship between climate change and CME by elucidating moral issues at their intersection. We begin by considering the dispersion of cause and effect in climate change, and we use this basis to address responsibilities and obligations related to climate and health. After these are outlined, we consider the central factors that disentangled and continue to separate CME from the environment.

### The Dispersion of Cause and Effect

The dispersion of cause and effect that leads to climate change raises questions regarding if individual responsibilities and obligations exist for its mitigation and management. In contrast with most issues that CME covers, climate change involves cumulative actions and consequences on a global and intergenerational scale.9 Dispersion, as it relates to climate change, covers two phenomena: (1) that actions contributing to climate change occur in one place or time and the effects in another, and (2) that single acts or individuals inconsequentially contribute to any one effect. For example, one person’s choice to bike or drive to work in Boston in 2023 may affect the likelihood or severity of a mudslide in Pakistan in 2065, but that individual effect is small, distant in time and space, and not individually predictable. As it relates to CME, dispersion asks if an individual can be held responsible for or have obligations to the climate we all share and, if they can, who are those individuals?

Moral philosophy is debating these questions. Arguments against individual responsibility include the lack of a clear causal chain,10,11 that climate change would continue irrespective of individual acts,12,13 and that responsibility cannot be assigned based on acts committed without knowledge of their harms.14 Rebuttals have been made from the standpoint of deontological, consequentialist, and virtue ethics. These include a duty to avoid generally knowable and foreseeable harms;15,16 that maximizing the good cannot be done without mitigating climate change;17 and that acting to mitigate climate change is virtuous.18,19 The first rebuttal argues that individual causes and effects need not be causally linked if the amalgam of causes contributes to a variety of harms, there are data showing emissions causally linked to harms through climate change, and humanity is aware of actions that propagate emissions. The second and third avoid the need for a causal basis altogether.

While there may never be consensus, the established arguments in favor of individual responsibility and obligation justify considering these issues relevant for CME. Perhaps as important, CME exists through its practical application, and many human beings receiving or providing healthcare consider themselves to be responsible for mitigating and managing climate change as it relates to health.20,21 A number of health professional organizations exist to address such problems. Within the United States, these include the Medical Society Consortium on Climate and Health, Center for Climate Change Communication, and C-CHANGE.22–24 The social norm indicated by this movement provides practical support for the environment as relevant for CME.

### Climate Responsibilities and Obligations Related to Health

If we grant an individual responsibility, which individuals are responsible for climate change, and should those who are be obliged to mitigate and manage it? Multiple approaches to these questions exist. The most established that are “polluters pay” on account of their contributions to climate change, “beneficiaries pay” because of the benefits they receive from actions that contribute to climate change, or the “advantaged pay” as they have the ability to do so.25,26 The relevant question for CME is if there are climate-related responsibilities and obligations related to healthcare practice. The two broad groups to be considered are those receiving healthcare and those providing it.

As they relate to receiving healthcare, responsibilities and obligations for climate change mitigation and management may be different in kind from other acts if certain conditions are met. These conditions are: Healthcare is considered a right.There is a clear distinction between acts of receiving healthcare and other acts.There is a clear distinction between acts of providing healthcare and other acts.Those receiving healthcare cannot mitigate or manage the environmental effects of their healthcare without negatively impacting that healthcare. Note: An individualistic definition of the person is assumed here because this most strongly argues for differences in kind as obviating climate-related responsibilities.

For healthcare acts that meet these conditions, responsibilities related to healthcare receipt may be diminished relative to other acts that do not meet parallel conditions (e.g., receiving adequate nutrition might also be considered a right and have distinct associated acts, but receiving a luxury wristwatch is not considered a right). Nonetheless, a responsibility to the environment can still exist without impacting the right itself. Moreover, even if healthcare is privileged relative to some acts, multiple theories of justice would accept a reduction in healthcare that negatively impacts an individual if such reductions are justified by other rights thought to be equally or more important, or lead to net positive utility, etc.

If human responsibilities exist, healthcare providers’ assumption of a fiduciary responsibility for humans’ health establishes a basis for their responsibility for climate change mitigation. This can be separated into two responsibilities. First is a general responsibility related to the impact of the practice of medicine on the environment. Second is an individual responsibility related to how their healthcare provision produces emissions (or allows them to benefit from pollution, or grants them an advantaged position). The specific basis and scope of climate-related obligations for individual healthcare providers, however, remains unclear. Before considering how moral theory (and CME) might address these questions, we discuss the ongoing separation of climate change and CME.

### CME and the Environment

Two factors have disentangled or maintained CME’s separation from the environment. The first is that the transdisciplinary nature of climate change has allowed CME to largely disregard it as a problem to be dealt with by other areas of bioethics and moral philosophy. These include the birth of bioethics with Van Rensselaer Potter,27 the early work of Pierce, Jameton,28 and Jamieson,19 and the recent work of Macpherson,29 Gardiner,30 Resnik,31 and Richie.32 Each has written eloquently on the essential bioethical nature of climate change and/or the environment, inclusive of human health. Some are based in moral philosophy and others public health ethics, where there is alignment but not synonymy with CME. Even with these efforts, modern CME qua CME has largely focused on human biomedicine, with climate concerns labelled environmental ethics.33–35

The other factor centers on CME’s anthropocentric focus. This problematic view has winnowed the operationalization of CME to those principals, rights, duties, virtues, and/or attendant outcomes as they relate to human parties involved in making human health decisions,36 with increasing consideration of general human health, such as issues arising during the COVID-19 pandemic. CME as is stands today rose to prominence alongside Beauchamp and Childress’s Principlism,37 and it has justified human health decisions chiefly based on those parties present in the clinical situation. This same scope has been used in other commonly applied CME systems such as those based in virtue.38 An inattention to ecology has left CME to neglect the complete meaning, rights, virtues, and consequences related to individual health decisions. At the same time, there is general agreement that responsible healthcare professionals should maintain obligations to help and avoid harming those for whom they care, respect their autonomy, and consider the fairness of their decisions. Maintaining an artificial separation through this approach is untenable.

Overall, these problems reflect CMEs lack of recognition that climate change and ecologic considerations are a necessary problem for the individual. They pose implicit questions for CME about provider and patient responsibilities and obligations to consider the environmental impact of human health decisions; how to maintain therapeutic relationships in the face of differing conceptions of those responsibilities and obligations; whether and how the pursuit of sustainability should limit health-related choices; and the degree to which healthcare providers’ professional responsibilities extend to environmental sustainability. We now consider how a revised scope for CME (“climate conscious CME”) might approach these issues, and how existing normative bases for CME may be redeployed.

## A Theoretical Basis for Climate Conscious Clinical Medical Ethics

### How Does Climate Change Alter the Scope of CME?

Accepting the entanglement of climate change and CME, and that the consequent issues outlined above should be reconciled, there are several paths forward. First is to decide if the scope of CME is appropriate or needs to be adjusted. Second is to identify how current approaches to CME account for ecologic concerns.

If we accept the premises of the prior section, the current scope of CME as “helping patients, families, physicians, and other health professionals reach good clinical decisions by taking into account both the specific clinical situation and the patient’s values and preferences”36 is incomplete. This definition does not account for the ecological context of clinical decisions or their consequences, and clinical medicine is implicitly divorced from those concerns. Climate conscious CME acknowledges how human traits, actions, or consequences (depending on one’s approach) extend beyond the clinic. It puts those concerns alongside, rather than implicitly subordinate to, clinical situations and the values and preferences of those present. This acknowledgement does not diminish the traits, actions, or consequences of those present. It recognizes that a patient is not isolated but instead a life entangled. At the same time, it elevates the life inadvertently diminished by CME—not at the expense of the patient—but for their mutual benefit.

Climate conscious CME “[helps] patients, families, physicians, and other health professionals reach good clinical decisions by taking into account … the specific clinical situation, … the patient’s values and preferences,” and how these decisions affect other human beings and the ecologic context in which they are made. This climate conscious scope gives all actors in clinical medicine responsibilities for other human beings and their ecosystem (for action-oriented systems) or says that those actors’ traits should account for other humans and the environment (for trait-based systems). It also raises the importance of human-human justice in CME, for which several theories have long argued,25,39 while moving beyond human beings as the only subjects of moral worth. This climate conscious scope directly intertwines CME with the environment rather than maintaining their separation, such as has been proposed through a public health “bridge”40 that accounts for the interaction of environment and health through system-level policies. Like the original scope of CME, a public health bridge alone does not address environmental concerns related to individual responsibility or virtue. Rather than cohesively aligning individual actors with other humans and their environment, an approach that only bridges clinic and environment through public health is adversarial: individual actors are free from environmental concerns that are instead mandated by the system. As discussed further in the section on climate justice, climate conscious public health ethics are necessary, not as a bridge, but as a complement to climate conscious CME.

With this climate conscious scope as a guide, we turn to several moral theories that act as common foundations for ethical clinical practice: virtue ethics, feminist ethics, and prominent theories of justice (consequentialism, egalitarianism, and capabilities theories). These theories are not presented to the exclusion of others, which may also be reasonable bases for climate conscious CME. Principlism is not presented independently as it draws from several of these foundational theories. This discussion is also not a complete account of the variety of thought that falls under each theory—or an attempt to establish a unified approach between them. We present these disparate theories to argue that each substantiates the need for clinical medicine to meet the challenges presented by climate change, and together, how they might change clinical medical practice.

### Climate Conscious Clinical Virtue Ethics

Virtues have compelling justifications through which environmentally accountable clinical practice might be approached. Traditional CME virtues have been defined as good, habituated character traits that promote acting well in response to clinical medical choices insofar as they promote the health of a patient.41 When expanded to accept that there are known climate-related impacts from medical care—which are detrimental to the each patient and others—traits can be redefined according both to their promotion of patient health and insofar as they also recognize environment implications. If a particular form of a trait does not sufficiently account for climate harms, a virtuous patient or healthcare provider would recognize and recalibrate their stance because not doing so would be insensitive to those harms. In this way, virtues avoid the tragedy of the commons; they are also not undercut by causal pathway arguments against individual responsibilities or inconsequentialism.18,42 For patients and providers, climate conscious virtue in CME would promote habituating health-related traits that minimize climate-related harms for themselves and others. Broadly speaking, virtues provide a starting point from which co-benefits can be approached: the pursuit of excellence of the individual receiving or providing healthcare for that individual, others, and the environment.

When we move from the general to the practical, concerns arise. There remains a lack of clear enumeration of what traits engender acting well in climate-conscious CME, and how they may be sufficient for medical care during morally ambiguous circumstances.43 How would clinical virtue ethics adequately direct compassion for the individual and compassion for humanity (or for non-human beings of moral worth) when compassion for one harms the other? It may be environmentally harmful to prescribe a medication at a patient’s request when there is another that is less ecologically toxic but equally safe and effective. While we recognize that this holds a virtue-based approach to a standard that it may never have intended to meet,44,45 clinical medicine is where tangible decisions are made, and without sufficient direction this criticism is reasonable. Climate-consciousness does not provide qualitatively different problems for a virtue-based approach to CME, but an additional set of problems that are morally ambiguous. It adds further complexity to these criticisms.

This approach may be most helpful for identifying choices and characteristics that are not virtuous, which clearly includes traits related to climate and health that harm patients, other humans, non-humans, and/or the environment. It also provides reasons why those with means and opportunity, such as healthcare professionals, should act well through their responses to climate change, and that because their opportunities to act are linked to their position as a healthcare professional, they have particular obligations to do so. The arguable obviation of direction in virtue ethics, however, may exacerbate common clinical ethical dilemmas by offering relativistic conceptions of environmental and health harms. Nonetheless, if pluralistic CME is the only answer for a problem so vast and complex as the ecological destruction of human life, virtues may serve as a basis from which to move forward.

### Climate Conscious Feminist Clinical Ethics

Feminist approaches to CME are well poised to address the problems of climate change. Feminist bioethics and environmental philosophy account for and are based upon concern for others and the environment.46 It is largely through the historic split of CME and biomedical ethics from environmental philosophy that feminist CME sometimes ignores non-human biota and ecologic concerns.47 Indeed, some approaches to feminist environmental philosophy (e.g., deep ecology) might take issue with CME as a defined field from the perspective that an ethic of human medical practice promotes patriarchal histories of androcentric dominance and culture-nature dualism.48 If CME is considered the practice of a larger ethic that spans human medicine and the environment, however, a climate conscious scope explicitly relates medical decisions to other humans and non-humans. It also acknowledges that CME has a perspective (from which biases and relationships can be identified) and undermines the domination of nature implicit in its prior scope.

The most widespread, feminist-informed aspects of modern CME are the ethics of care,49,50 which is popularly defined through the qualities of attentiveness, responsibility, competence, responsiveness, and solidarity, and a form of relational autonomy where the capacity for self-determination is based on and not comprised by relationships.51 To maintain the connection of medical practice with its environmental complement, CME care qualities should be understood as encompassing humanity and the environment rather than applied only to those present in the clinic and their immediate social context. The ethics of care is based in, or at least aligned with, an ecofeminist ethic that would reject the separation of those present in a medical situation and those not present but harmed (or helped) as a consequence of the situation’s effects, environmental or otherwise. Neither should the recognition of a human medical need; having accountability, adeptness, and understanding of that need; and meeting that need collectively be used to promote culture-nature dualism.46 Indeed, the ethics of care might be best maintained as a climate conscious CME system through a definition of relational autonomy that is based upon both human and non-human relationships.

Climate conscious relational autonomy is one that extends beyond human relationships and their related sense of identity that have sometimes been used to define its scope.47,52 The autonomy of those involved in a clinical situation would be grounded in their interrelationships and interdependence, the extension of those concepts to other humans (both individuals and humanity at-large), and to Leopold’s “land” (meaning the soils, waters, plants, and animals).53 It would also be based in the sense of identity held by those individuals as it extends into human society and the land in which they exist. With this extended scope of relational autonomy, the broader definitions of care qualities are clearer. This scope requires attentiveness, responsibility, competence, responsiveness, and solidarity to meet the need of the person within their social and environmental context, accounting for the human and non-human together as parts of the clinical milieu.47,52 Notably, this account of autonomy asks those involved in the receipt or provision of healthcare to resist the structures that have separated the clinic from lived experience and person from environment. The need for such resistance underscores Principlist CMEs longstanding presumption of atomistic autonomy.54 Under the dominance of Principlism, CME has assumed few responsibilities or obligations toward those outside of the clinical scenario (excepting specific circumstances), and it has asked those who demand this of clinical medicine to provide the burden of proof. A relational approach inverts this, beginning with interdependence and views critically exceptions to that basis.

Notably, our account of climate conscious care ethics and relational autonomy build on current feminist shifts in clinical medicine such as recognizing patients as existing as part of a social network and rejecting a societal structure that determines and often dominates those who have been marginalized. It extends those networks and structures to the land, providing a holistic basis for responsibilities. By asking healthcare professionals to consider this larger scope of person-in-environment, it also eliminates any separation between responsibility for patient and responsibility for environmental sustainability and conservation. One difficulty for this approach lies in how to apply these responsibilities and obligations equitably across the inequitable medical structures that currently exist. This answer may be in solidarity. Through solidarity, individuals’ recognized inequities in social determinants of health, and their collective action to remediate these inequities is underway.55 A similar movement appears to be starting for environmental determinants.56

### Climate Conscious Clinical Justice

Approaches to climate justice have been substantiated through moral theories that are widely applied in CME.39,57–60 Consequentialism mandates climate action that maximizes good outcomes, with gains in marginal utility greatest for those most vulnerable to climate effects. The communitarian approach recognizes the threat of climate change to society and each other, obligating humans to collectively safeguard the commons.61 Capabilities theorists have linked human well-being with the environment, setting standards that account for variations in baseline needs and climate change contributions.62 Most applications of these theories have appropriately focused on justice at the systems level. Debate has focused on the uncertainty of future benefits and burdens, related intergenerational responsibilities, how those responsibilities might be shared, and non-compliance by nation states.63–65 Their application to CME has been limited. Below, we review the context in which this gap has persisted as well as how climate justice theory applies to clinical medical practice.

The gap between climate justice theories and CME exists for at least two reasons. The first is historical, in that ecologic concerns exist only at the margins of CME’s dominant Principlist framework. Principlism’s account of autonomy is anthropocentric and individualistic, and in practice preeminent over other principles.66 By extension, it has disentangled common conceptions of justice in CME from burdens experienced by those outside healthcare—and often for those outside the clinical situation at hand.67 A shift toward justice as being between and among a web of life is beginning, and these versions of justice resist Principlist conceptions.68,69 To date, however, they remain outside mainstream CME.

The second reason is that, as applications of climate change mitigation move from the system to individual level (i.e., toward clinical practice), they become necessarily more inconsistent, exacerbating injustice. One answer to this is the public health bridge that brings together environmental and clinical concerns, promoting just standards of health that incorporate both.40,70 This aligns with the earlier discussion of some aspects of healthcare as a qualitatively privileged good; public health is well positioned to assign standards for this good such that its application is consistent. This system-level approach to climate change is also essential for breaking out of Western healthcare’s treat-harm-treat cycle (i.e., treating individual humans but harming the environment, which then harms humans, who then require more treatment),71 and for approaching intergenerational justice concerns, which are inherently systems-level.

System-level mitigation and management is a complement, and arguably a prerequisite, for individual mitigation and management. Individual change absent system change will be heterogeneous and exacerbate injustice. System-level responsibility, however, can be only a complement or prerequisite for individual-level responsibility, not a replacement. Indeed, system-level responses are necessarily composed of, and enacted by, individuals.42 If individual health provision and receipt is provided without consideration of its place in the environment, decisions that are not optimal for humans (and non-humans and the environment) will continue. Such statements are also supported by data demonstrating the climate impact of individual human health decisions and health-related lifestyle choices (e.g., inhalers, telehealth use, veganism).72–76 Alone, the public health approach also insufficiently examines what should be done when standards cannot be met locally (i.e., scarce resource allocation) or are not followed by individuals (i.e., non-compliance), which are common applications of justice for CME.

So, alongside a public health standard, what responsibilities do existing theories of justice promote for clinical practice and the individuals involved? We previously discussed healthcare providers’ fiduciary responsibility to minimize health harms or promote virtues that do the same. This begets climate-associated duties or traits. If a provider’s duty is to health or well-being, or if they habituate traits toward that goal, minimizing climate-related harms is part of that duty or trait. Theories of justice define specific justifications upon which that minimization is based as well as the scope of what is to be minimized. Established bases for provider responsibility (through their role as polluter, beneficiary, or with the ability to pay) can each be justified through egalitarian-, contractual-, and utility-based means, among others.25,26 While strong normative alignment exists between specific theories and bases for responsibility, with harm minimization as the goal, the pluralism of CME suggests that whichever basis is most effective and reasonably practical should be used. Since minimization occurs in non-ideal settings, we discuss how non-compliance with responsibilities might be approached in the Supplemental Appendix and below in a section on politicization.

As public health is well positioned to guide just health standards that account for environmental concerns, justice demands for CME should be aligned, complementary, and strike balance between any injustice their heterogenous application might cause and the harm their lack of application would incur. This scope defines CME-related responsibility to be most justifiable in areas of practice where the health standard is not impinged, and environmental harms can be minimized. Examples include utilizing or advocating for alternative care strategies that equally meet the health standard (e.g., prescribing a clinically equivalent medicine that has fewer climate harms, petitioning administrators for more sustainable care delivery practices) and eliminating practices that cause environmental harms and either lack sufficient scientific bases (e.g., whole body magnetic resonance imaging for cancer-screening) and/or are performed for reasons beyond health promotion or related well-being (e.g., some types of cosmesis). In these areas, heterogeneous application would be minimally unjust as the health standard would be maintained and additional health would be promoted indirectly. Given that the latter two practices are disproportionately available to the affluent, their modification or elimination arguably promotes egalitarian and contractarian justice even absent environmental concerns. CME-related responsibilities are also most justified where traits or acts performed are second-order, meaning they promote climate mitigation/adaptation through or with others rather than directly.77 This is because second-order acts influence others and thus are less subject to claims of injustice through heterogeneity.

A CME-specific responsibility to limit or redistribute a public health standard for the purposes of climate-related harm reduction would generally not be supported by theories of justice. This, however, does not obviate clinical medicine from its responsibility to adopt public health standards that minimize environmental harms. Neither does it free them from commitments to minimize environmental harms that do not impinge upon the health standard. Moreover, at least two settings exist in which there are CME-specific responsibilities related to climate justice: when standards cannot be met locally (i.e., scarce resource allocation) or are not followed by individuals (i.e., non-compliance). We address these situations, and the environmental connections for the justice theories commonly applied to them, in the Supplemental Appendix.

These theories, alongside virtue and feminist ethics, justify revising the scope of CME. With this basis, we outline an approach for climate conscious clinical ethics.

## Climate Conscious CME in Practice

A revised scope for CME aligns with existing moral theory and develops an ethic of medical practice that promotes human health while acknowledging that each person exists in relation to others and the environment. Jonsen and Siegler’s Clinical Ethics provided the definition of CME stated at the beginning of the article; their Four Topics model (medical indications, preferences of patients, quality of life, and contextual features) is a widely used, practice-oriented operationalization of CME.36 Through this approach, based in Principlism, climate change and environmental concerns would be considered wholly as “contextual features.” Under climate conscious CME, we propose an update. We discuss changes to the Topics and related practices as the Climate Conscious Four Topics model, and we provide an updated approach to clinical situations (Table 1).

Some points are worth noting beforehand. First, this model is intended for healthcare provider use. While we also discussed healthcare recipients above, the proposed model maintains a clinician perspective for clarity and consistency. Second, the original CME model presents information to the reader as an atomistic individual. Our modified approach implicitly shifts this, presenting CME to providers as human beings who exist and practice in the context of their community and environment. Third, as the original Topics are justified through Principlism, Topics have been altered to align with the expanded scope of CME and justified through previously discussed moral theories. Fourth, while this focuses on clinical interactions, climate-related clinician responsibilities exist outside such interactions, such as advocating for climate conscious practice to administrators and policymakers.34 Fifth, while the revised Topics entangle climate and health, they do not demand clinicians do so at the expense of all other responsibilities, but alongside them. Surely, it would be inappropriate to offer a patient with incurable but treatable cancer only supportive care, even if this leads to the least emissions, or to burden them by discussing such a duty. Finally, the Four Topics is only one operational approach to CME; its use is not to the exclusion of other approaches but to show how to ecologically entangle the concepts discussed above with medical practice.

### Indications for Care

Medical Indications are the underlying reasons for human medical care and are a reasonable beginning from which to assess most clinical situations. The original definition of Indications was, “the facts and their interpretations about the patient’s physical and/or psychological condition that provide a reasonable basis for the physician’s clinical judgments aiming to realize the overall goals of medicine: prevention, cure, and treatment of illness and injury.” This definition reflects an atomistic and physiologic account of the person, and it focuses only on negative conditions. It does not address how the condition was precipitated in relation to others and the environment, how those things might have contributed to or eased the condition, the related experience of life, and other recognized goals of medicine.

Climate conscious CME seeks to explicitly consider and address those underlying entanglements. Rather than focusing on the medical indication of “heat stroke caused by prolonged exposure,” the medical indication becomes, “exhaustion from heat stroke, caused by climate change and outdoor work, for the primary caregiver of a multi-generational family in a rural setting.” Moreover, by only seeking remedy of illness and injury, the current definition does not align with the goals of medical practice that climate change demands. At minimum, the goal has become ecologically sustainable human health promotion. Some approaches might demand a higher standard, such as human and ecological thriving.

A revised “Indications for Care” could instead read, “the medical facts, their connection to the patient’s social, natural, and built environment and lived experience, and their interpretations, which together provide a reasonable basis for the clinicians’ clinical judgments, aiming to realize the overall goals of medicine: ecologically sustainable prevention, cure, treatment of illness and injury, and the promotion of health” (italics indicate changes). This revision accounts for the experiences of those involved, their environment, and the role of medicine as attending to human health while deliberately incorporating other beings and the environment, which previously existed outside its scope. The specific inclusion of “experience” more closely ties Indications for Care to Quality of Life, as below. Through this definition, an approach to assessing Indications is amended as outlined in Table 1. Questions now account for sustainability, downstream negative impacts on human and ecologic health, and the underlying relationships between the condition of the person and their environment.

### Preferences and Commitments

The next topic, Preferences of Patients, is defined as, “the choices that persons make when they are faced with decisions about health and medical treatment.” The topic focuses on the individual and artificially isolates the decision-making. In practice, the person with the medical problem will have preferences that need to be addressed. The above sections, however, describe why preferences and considerations beyond the individual should be simultaneously and not only subordinately considered. These include human beings connected to the patient, clinicians, and other humans and non-humans who can be impacted by their care. There is also the question of other types of beings, inanimate things, and future beings (who some argue cannot have preferences).

Breaking from the original Four Topics, the Preferences of Patients becomes Preferences, which now focuses on those who can express preferences, meaning they are involved in the clinical situation and have the ability to express preference to each other (e.g., the patient, clinicians, and other humans connected to the situation through either). Contextual Features changes to Commitments, which reflects an equal need to assess and incorporate the preferences of those who are not directly involved and/or unable to voice preferences, and the commitments of those who can express preferences to the environment within which care is provided. Commitments, rather than responsibility, also acknowledges grounding in virtue and care.

Preferences divided from Commitments is not a restatement of the original Topics of Preferences of Patients and Contextual Features. This revision acknowledges that, in practice, those who can state preferences are different from those who cannot: the latter are of special concern because their preferences or concerns can be easily overridden, and at the same time, they are not merely context but should be thought of as entangled with those present—and as equally essential. In this way Commitments is analogous to how CME has traditionally approached proxy decision-making. They are the commitments of those who can state preferences acting as proxies for those who cannot, including non-humans. It also recognizes that those who can express preferences are able to do so through connections to each other, to others beyond, and are doing so within their environment. In the context of clinical practice and because of the theory outlined above, they are intrinsically committed through responsibilities and virtues.

In this approach, climate conscious CME continues to include questions of situational understanding (e.g., capacity, consent) to all those involved. It extends what is encompassed in that understanding to include benefits and risks of diagnosis and treatment beyond their effect on the patient. Preferences also asks questions of non-compliance related to the risks and benefits of care. This allows agreement and disagreements about health decisions to encompass disagreements about treatment between the human beings present alongside disagreements related to consequences for others and the environment. There is related debate over “green consent” (i.e., discussing environmental concerns during decision-making) as obligatory or optional, beneficial or politicized and distracting.78–80 Depending on one’s conception of autonomy, all can be true, with the former based in relational autonomy and the latter a Principlist conception. Indeed, in a Principlist dominated world, climate conscious CME is politicized and distracting. As this is the case in many Western countries, approaches to non-compliance are key (see Supplemental Appendix). Nonetheless, we submit that politicization is not an unsurmountable barrier between moral theory and CME. Relative to the original Topic, Preferences includes the interests of all those directly involved in the case as they relate to each other, not only those of the patient.

Commitments focuses on operationalizing responsibilities or virtues related to the receipt or provision of medical care, especially toward those unable to express preference, and in that way aligns with the understanding asked about in Preferences. Yet it remains distinct in that it asks what commitments those who are directly involved have as a result of receiving or providing care. Commitments grounds the patient’s life in its web of socio-ecological connection. Such connections are implicit commitments and, as they relate to the medical situation at hand, are a substantive part of clinical decision-making. Professional and general medical Commitments related to ecology stem from the justifications discussed in climate justice. This Topic also covers more traditionally discussed commitments in CME such as to country and laws, religion, research practice, and integrity. Overriding commitments does not necessarily require a higher or lower standard than that of preferences, but it is different in that it requires those who are involved account for their implicit or explicit commitments to those who unable to do so, including non-humans.

### Quality of Life

In the original Four Topics, Quality of Life, “refers to that degree of satisfaction that people experience and value about their lives as a whole, and in its particular aspects, such as physical and psychological health. [Ethical] dimensions … include … beneficence as help, … autonomy, … [and] beneficence as satisfaction …” Similar to Medical Indications, this is a largely anthropocentric approach. At the same time, ignoring this would violate central tenants of a number of moral theories, including the ethics of care and virtue-based approaches.

Like Medical Indications, what Quality of Life is and encompasses must be reconciled with the expanded scope of CME. Quality of Life as a concept that describes the experience of healthy living (or lack thereof) is immediately applicable to other humans beyond the patient; arguments by Singer and Regan have extended this to non-humans.81,82 Health as, “how well [a part or process of a living thing] measures up to the demands of the moment, and a matter of its capacity or disposition to make a specific contribution when it is needed,”83 also encompasses all of these beings. Climate conscious Quality of Life continues to ask about the health state of the patient, their experiences of that state, and what is done to assess and manage that state out of respect for their experiences (Table 1). Extending those questions beyond the individual patient allows both patient and provider to consider how the Indications for Care change the experience of others directly and indirectly related to the case, and what detriments to quality might be wrought by the care provided. This reflects the Ethics of Care and maintains the experience of autonomy as relational, more closely tying Quality of Life to Indications for Care as reflecting the reasons, virtues, intentions, and goals considered during clinical care.

Compared to the original Four Topics, this climate conscious version operationalizes the processes of medical care through Indications for Care and Quality of Life and the perspectives of the life affected by that care through Processes and Commitments. In this way, each pair is not separate but linked, each aspect incomplete without the other. Processes and Commitments are defined by Indications and Quality, and Indications and Quality realized through Processes and Commitments. Each should be approached with a recognition that there is bias from the human medical viewpoint, and that through virtue and/or responsibility, all those not involved directly remain intimately connected and impacted by this care.

## Conclusion

The ethical problems wrought by climate change are substantial. They have clear importance for clinical medical practice, which itself impacts the environment. Thus far, CME has divided human and environmental health. Our exploration shows why and how CME can meet the challenge of climate change while continuing to guide medical practice.

There are two avenues by which to begin this process. The first is medical education, where the next generation of healthcare providers can be taught climate conscious CME as encompassing patients, others, and the land together. Our medical school has already enacted a climate curriculum for students to understand connection between health and ecology; beginning this year their medical ethics courses will begin to include some of the concepts discussed herein. The second is hospital ethics committees. These committees should continue to build connections to other organizational structures that promote climate and health within and outside of their institution, such as sustainability committees and the climate and health organizations mentioned earlier. They can together help guide hospital policy on the need for sustainable care, aide practitioners in understanding their roles and responsibilities, and approach ethics consults through climate conscious CME. Together, such change can inform medical practice that repairs the rend between person and environment.

Our approach leaves many topics to be explored. These includes how theories of justice (e.g., well-being or capabilities approaches) might further imbue medical practice with climate obligations; which climate-relation actions for professionals are ideal versus obligatory; and how to approach specific scenarios of conflict between harms for the patient and the environment. Nonetheless, through ecologically conscious clinical virtue, an ethic of care, relational autonomy, and climate justice there exist deep commitments to the environment that clinical medicine must meet and are aligned with its purpose.
